title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is a personal AI assistant deployed in private testing that connects to users' emails, messaging apps, calendars, and devices to perform tasks on their behalf. Early testers found the system could be phished to gain unauthorized access, continued operating after users thought they had disconnected it, and sent emails on users' behalf without explicit approval. These failures show what happens when an AI system with broad access to personal data and the ability to act autonomously is deployed without sufficient safeguards.

The deployment lacked controls that would have caught these problems before release. An explicit approval step before the system takes actions on a user's behalf would have prevented unauthorized emails. Monitoring and logging of what the system accesses after disconnection would have revealed the continued summarization. Testing against common attack vectors like phishing would have identified the unauthorized access vulnerability. The terms of service granted the company broad rights to user data for training, compounding the security issues.

Whether these failures resulted from inadequate security design, insufficient testing, or other causes is not established from the reporting.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
# Summary

Instinct, a powerful AI personal assistant currently in private testing, is generating excitement for its impressive capabilities but also raising significant privacy and security concerns. The San Francisco-based platform, created by former Sierra research scientist Noah Shinn and operated by Spear Street Technology, connects to users' emails, messaging apps, calendars, devices, and more to handle tasks like booking appointments, scheduling rides, and organizing inboxes. However, early testers have identified troubling issues, including overly broad terms of service that grant the company perpetual rights to user data for training purposes, difficulty deleting stored emails, and the ability to act on users' behalf without explicit approval.

Security experts and early adopters have raised alarms about giving AI this level of access. One user discovered Instinct could be easily phished to gain unauthorized access, while another found the system continued summarizing emails after disconnecting. A venture capitalist noted Instinct sent an email on her behalf without permission, breaking her trust. The company, backed by investors including Kleiner Perkins and Conviction, has not responded publicly to the concerns but told The Wall Street Journal it is raising a $250 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation led by Index Ventures and Benchmark.
